summary: Sungkyunkwan University authors encode regulations as executable Python compliance code. GPT-5 decomposes each provision into atomic yes/no/None checklist variables organized by Kelsen's four spheres of validity, fills a code template, and runs a self-verification loop that scores the code 0-5 on five criteria for up to 10 iterations. A small model (Qwen2.5 7B, 1.5B or 0.5B) then answers the checklist questions against a case, and the code decides violation per article. Evaluation covers the EU AI Act and GDPR (PrivaCI-Bench), a new set of 406 Korean PIPA deliberation decisions summarized by GPT-5, and two LegalBench tasks. The paper reports the best F1 against direct prompting and four published symbolic encodings that the authors rebuilt with GPT-5. This is legal compliance reasoning, not software development.

claims.claim: Code-as-Auditor achieves the highest F1 on all three frameworks, beating the second-best method by +3.1 (EU AI Act), +3.4 (GDPR) and +12.3 (PIPA)
claims.evidence: Table 4 with Qwen2.5-7B over three trials matches: 90.7 vs 87.6, 61.2 vs 57.8, 55.3 vs 43.0. All baselines were re-implemented by the authors with GPT-5-generated representations. Only recall and F1 are reported, not precision. Direct prompting has higher recall on the EU AI Act (96.0 vs 84.5) and PIPA (87.5 vs 80.0). The PIPA dataset is the authors' own.

claims.claim: The approach stays robust with smaller inference models while tuple- and logic-based encodings degrade
claims.evidence: Table 5 gaps are large (e.g., EU AI Act at 0.5B: 86.0 vs 49.4/27.2). However, the baselines are reported as averages over two methods each ('Tuple', 'Logic'), not as the best single baseline, and direct prompting is omitted from this table.

claims.claim: The method generalizes beyond privacy law and outperforms frontier reasoning models on LegalBench
claims.evidence: Table 6: Telemarketing 92.0±0.4 vs GPT-5 90.7±1.2; SARA 82.7±3.1 vs GPT-5 Mini 81.3±1.1. Both margins are within about one standard deviation over three runs. GPT-5 also built the code being compared against GPT-5. Only two tasks.

claims.claim: Every component (checklist refinement, code template, self-verification loop) is necessary
claims.evidence: Fig. 8 over three trials. Removing self-verification gives zero on every metric only because the generated code no longer parses, so the ablation shows that the loop fixes syntax, not that it improves the reasoning. The checklist-refinement ablation (recall -18.65 GDPR, -37.91 PIPA) is the informative one.
Fig. 6 sweeps the loop depth and shows a plateau near 10, then a decline (PIPA -16.3 at 14). The default of 10 was chosen from this curve on the same evaluation data, and there is no held-out split.

patterns.note: Within the legal domain only: a machine-readable domain encoding (atomic checklist variables plus executable rules with explicit unknowns) beats direct prompting and four published symbolic encodings under the same inference model (Tables 4-5). Baselines are author re-implementations.

Each provision is linked to code and each checklist variable to a source clause. The paper itself states the loop certifies a well-formed decision procedure, not that the code preserves the statute's meaning, so the links are checked for form only.
A model verifier scores the generated code 0-5 on necessity, atomicity, hierarchy, completeness and syntax to drive refinement. The verifier's scores are never compared with expert judgment.
Regulations are decomposed into structured, binary-answerable conditions along who/what/when/where dimensions before evaluation.

methodology.sample: EU AI Act and GDPR test cases from PrivaCI-Bench (counts not restated); 406 Korean PIPC deliberation decisions; two LegalBench tasks (Telemarketing, SARA)
methodology.baselines: Direct prompting; CI Parameter, Deontic Triplet, PolicyLR and Semantic FOL, all re-implemented with GPT-5-built representations; GPT-5, GPT-5 Mini, Claude Sonnet 4.5 and Opus 4.5 on LegalBench only
methodology.models: GPT-5 builds all representations and the PIPA case summaries; Qwen2.5-7B/1.5B/0.5B perform inference
methodology.ablations: Removal of checklist refinement, code template and self-verification loop (Fig. 8); loop-depth sweep (Fig. 6); five alternative checklist decompositions (Fig. 7)
methodology.contamination_controls: None. Compliance labels come from published adjudications that may be in training data, and GPT-5 summaries were written to contain the 'central legal points at issue'.
methodology.languages: Generated Python compliance code; regulations in English and Korean

standards.artifacts: None released (no code or dataset link)

biases.detail: The authors built the PIPA dataset and re-implemented every baseline themselves.
The self-verification loop relies on model-assigned 0-5 scores that are never checked against legal experts.
The iteration count of 10 and the design choices were selected from curves on the same evaluation sets.
No code, prompts or the 406-case PIPA dataset are released.
Recall and F1 are reported without precision, and the article-level match does not test whether the code preserves statutory meaning, as the authors concede.
GPT-5 summaries of already-adjudicated decisions were written to contain the central legal points, which may leak the outcome and smooth away distractors (partly acknowledged under 'Dataset Bias').

verdict_reason: Off-topic: LLM legal-compliance reasoning over regulation text, not software development with agents or its human side. On its own terms, the gains rest on author-rebuilt baselines and an author-built, unreleased dataset with model-written case summaries. The LegalBench margins are within noise, the loop depth was tuned on the test curves, and the self-verification ablation measures syntax repair rather than reasoning quality.
applicability: Only a loose analogy for the Java team. Encoding domain rules (for example, domain constraints) as atomic yes/no checks with an explicit 'unknown' value, so that the unknowns list exactly what a spec still needs, is a reasonable idea for a domain card. This paper gives no evidence that it helps software agents or developers, and its own discussion warns that a well-formed encoding is not a faithful one. Any such rule encoding would need expert review of the meaning, not just a passing self-check.
